shots.why: process one, tight: piston rings seated by hand, 1936, its own factory score. Tight on purpose; the man comes back later.
process two: mallet and stool, a 1941 re-enactment of frontier work, its narrator kept.
process three, a woman at a tire-bead machine, 1934, reaching over and over.
coordination begins: a sung work verse from a 1951 film takes over. With a mallet in his hand.
cut on the sung beat: these hands are not holding a mallet, and the song does not know that.
cut on the sung beat; the tire worker is also inside the carpenter's song for one second.
back to the mallet as the verse ends. Coordination lasts seven seconds and is never repeated.
coordination broken by a hard cut. A refinery worker wipes his hands and holds a valve wheel, in his own time, at normal speed, with his film's voice.
the interval, whole and at normal speed: a man looks into a machine, then reaches up into it. Nothing is produced.
waiting: a man stands while hot rail runs past him. Belo Horizonte, 1949, not Detroit, and his narrator says so.
return to process one, wider: there was a face, and another man's arm, the whole time.
end: the old man reaches away from the block and the mallet is down.
end: a hand, stopped. Last frame held.
